props.title: The Devil Thumbs a Ride
props.initialSlug: Killer hitches ride, terrorizes innocent drivers

sections.content: The Devil Thumbs a Ride (1947) epitomizes film noir's fascination with chance encounters that spiral into nightmare scenarios. Lawrence Tierney's chilling performance as murderer Steve Morgan established him as noir's go-to heavy, rivaling similar menacing hitchhiker tales like Detour (1945). Director Felix E. Feist crafts a lean 62-minute thriller that wastes no time, opening with a bank robbery-murder and maintaining white-knuckle tension as an unsuspecting good Samaritan picks up the wrong passenger. The film's claustrophobic car sequences influenced later road thrillers like The Hitch-Hiker (1953) and Collateral (2004). The Hitch-Hiker|1953|Ida Lupino directs this taut noir about two friends held captive by a psychotic hitchhiker|Tubi Detour|1945|A down-on-his-luck pianist's cross-country trip turns deadly after picking up a mysterious woman|Prime Gun Crazy|1950|A sharp-shooting couple goes on a crime spree in this influential noir road movie|HBO Max

Tierney's portrayal of Morgan represents noir's quintessential psychopath - charming on the surface but harboring deadly intentions. His performance influenced countless noir villains, particularly in road-based crime films like Gun Crazy (1950) and They Live By Night (1948). The film's exploration of postwar American anxiety about strangers and the dark side of mobility resonated deeply with audiences still processing WWII trauma. SUBHEAD: The Hitchhiker in Film Noir

The hitchhiker became a powerful noir symbol, representing fate's cruel randomness and America's postwar mobility anxiety. Films like Stranger on the Third Floor (1940) and Beyond the Forest (1949) used hitchhiking sequences to introduce chaos into ordered lives. This tradition continued through neo-noir classics like The Hitcher (1986) and Joy Ride (2001), maintaining the hitchhiker as cinema's ultimate symbol of stranger danger.
